question: Which statement about 'Class 1', 'Class 2', 'Class A' and 'Class B' is correct?

options.text: Class 1 and Class 2 are activity permits; Class A and Class B are classes of UA pilot licence
options.why: Activity permits (AP1, AP2) authorise an activity at a place and time. UAPL classes (A, B) authorise a pilot to fly UA up to or above 25 kg.

options.text: Class 1 and Class A are the same thing; Class 2 and Class B are the same thing
options.why: They belong to different systems. Numbers are for activity permits, letters are for pilot licences.

options.text: Class A and Class B are activity permits for business and recreation
options.why: Business vs recreation is what separates AP1 from AP2 situations. Class A and B are licence classes based on UA mass.

options.text: Class 2 is the upgraded version of Class 1
options.why: Neither permit is an upgrade of the other. AP1 covers business, heavier or BVLOS flying; AP2 covers recreation or education under specific location and height conditions.

note: Numbers = permits for the ACTIVITY. Letters = licence for the PILOT.

question: What does a Class A UAPL allow, compared with a Class B UAPL?

options.text: Class A: any UA in the licensed category up to 25 kg. Class B: specific UA models over 25 kg
options.why: Class A covers any UA in its category with total mass not exceeding 25 kg. Class B covers specific models (ratings) above 25 kg.

options.text: Class A: UA up to 7 kg. Class B: UA from 7 kg to 25 kg
options.why: 7 kg is the mass above which a UAPL becomes mandatory for any purpose. Class A and B are split at 25 kg.

options.text: Class A: recreational flying. Class B: commercial flying
options.why: The licence class depends on UA mass, not purpose. Purpose decides which permit you need.

options.text: Class A: any category of UA. Class B: one category only
options.why: Both classes are issued per category (aeroplane, rotorcraft, powered-lift, airship). Class B is narrower still: it is rated for specific models.

question: A pilot wants a Class B UAPL to fly a 40 kg multirotor. What must they already hold?

options.text: Nothing; Class B is a stand-alone licence for heavy UA
options.why: Class B has a prerequisite. It is built on an existing Class A in the same category.

options.text: A valid Class A UAPL in the aeroplane category
options.why: The prerequisite must be in the CORRESPONDING category. A multirotor is a rotorcraft, not an aeroplane.

options.text: A valid Class A UAPL in the rotorcraft category, without any mass limitations
options.why: AC 101-4-1 gives exactly this example: a Class B for a 40 kg rotorcraft needs a valid Class A rotorcraft UAPL without mass limitations first.

options.text: A UA basic training certificate and a Class 1 Activity Permit
options.why: Basic training covers 1.5–7 kg recreational or educational flying, and a permit authorises an activity. Neither is a licence prerequisite.

question: Under which UAPL category does a quadcopter fall?

options.text: Powered-lift
options.why: Powered-lift is for UA that take off vertically and then fly on wings, such as VTOL fixed-wing hybrids.

options.text: Rotorcraft
options.why: The rotorcraft category includes helicopters and multirotors such as quadcopters and octocopters.

options.text: Multirotor, which is a separate fifth category
options.why: There are only four categories: aeroplane, rotorcraft, powered-lift and airship. Multirotors sit inside rotorcraft.

options.text: Aeroplane
options.why: Aeroplane is for fixed-wing UA that get lift from wings in forward flight.

question: A hobbyist flies a 10 kg UA for recreation in an open field, below 200 ft AMSL, more than 5 km from any aerodrome and outside restricted, danger and prohibited areas. What do they need?

options.text: A Class 2 Activity Permit and a UA basic training certificate
options.why: None of the AP2 conditions applies here. Basic training only covers 1.5–7 kg; above 7 kg a UAPL is required instead.

options.text: A UA Operator Permit and a Class 1 Activity Permit
options.why: For recreation, OP + AP1 is only needed above 25 kg or for BVLOS. A 10 kg recreational flight is below that.

options.text: Nothing, because no permit condition applies
options.why: No permit is needed, but the pilot still needs a licence: a UAPL is mandatory for any UA over 7 kg, whatever the purpose.

options.text: No permit, but a UAPL (and the UA must be registered)
options.why: Recreation at 25 kg or less needs a permit only under AP2 conditions, and none apply. But reg 35 requires a UAPL for any UA over 7 kg, and a UA over 250 g must be registered.

note: Permits follow the ACTIVITY and place; the licence follows the PILOT and the mass. Check both separately.

question: A school club flies a 10 kg UA for an education purpose in an open field, below 200 ft AMSL and away from aerodromes. What is required?

options.text: A Class 2 Activity Permit only
options.why: AP2 covers education only with UA of 7 kg or less, and only under AP2 conditions. At 10 kg the rules move to OP + AP1.

options.text: A UA Operator Permit, a Class 1 Activity Permit and a UAPL
options.why: Education with a UA over 7 kg (up to 25 kg) needs OP + AP1 under reg 8(3), wherever it flies. Any UA over 7 kg also needs a UAPL.

options.text: Nothing, because educational flying is exempt
options.why: Education has its own thresholds: AP2 conditions up to 7 kg, OP + AP1 above 7 kg.

options.text: A UA basic training certificate only
options.why: Basic training covers 1.5–7 kg. Above 7 kg the pilot needs a UAPL, and this activity also needs OP + AP1.

note: Education threshold is 7 kg; recreation threshold is 25 kg.

question: A hobbyist flies a 30 kg UA for recreation, within visual line of sight, in an open field. What is required?

options.text: A Class 2 Activity Permit and a Class A UAPL
options.why: AP2 only applies up to 25 kg, and a Class A UAPL only covers UA up to 25 kg.

options.text: A Class A UAPL only, because it is recreational
options.why: Recreation does not avoid permits above 25 kg: reg 7 requires OP + AP1 for any UA over 25 kg, for any purpose.

options.text: A UA Operator Permit, a Class 1 Activity Permit and a Class B UAPL for that model
options.why: Any UA over 25 kg needs OP + AP1 for any purpose (reg 7). Flying it needs a UAPL, and above 25 kg that is a Class B rated for the specific model.

options.text: A UA Operator Permit and a Class 2 Activity Permit
options.why: OP is always paired with AP1, never AP2.

question: A freelancer is paid to take photos with a 249 g drone in a park far from any aerodrome, below 200 ft AMSL. What is required?

options.text: Nothing, because the drone is under 250 g
options.why: 250 g only decides registration. Business use needs OP + AP1 and a UAPL regardless of mass.

options.text: A UA Operator Permit, a Class 1 Activity Permit and a UAPL (Class A, rotorcraft)
options.why: Business flying needs OP + AP1 regardless of mass (reg 9), and a UAPL for UA of any mass flown for business (reg 35(1)(a)).

options.text: A Class 2 Activity Permit, because the drone is light
options.why: AP2 is only for recreation or education. Business flying always needs OP + AP1.

options.text: A UA basic training certificate
options.why: Basic training only applies to recreation or education with UA over 1.5 kg up to 7 kg.

question: A hobbyist flies a 3 kg drone for recreation within 5 km of Seletar Airport. What is required?

options.text: A Class 2 Activity Permit, plus a UA basic training certificate (or a UAPL)
options.why: Within 5 km of an aerodrome is an AP2 condition for recreation up to 25 kg. A pilot of a 1.5–7 kg UA for recreation needs basic training or a UAPL (reg 33).

options.text: A UA Operator Permit and a Class 1 Activity Permit, because it is near an airport
options.why: Location never triggers OP + AP1. For recreation, being near an aerodrome triggers AP2.

options.text: A Class 2 Activity Permit and a Class B UAPL
options.why: Class B is for UA over 25 kg. At 3 kg, basic training or a Class A UAPL covers the pilot.

options.text: No permit, because 3 kg is a light UA
options.why: Mass doesn't remove the location condition. Any recreational UA up to 25 kg within 5 km of an aerodrome needs AP2.

question: An inspection company flies a 2 kg drone within 5 km of Paya Lebar Air Base. Which permits does it need?

options.text: A Class 2 Activity Permit, because the flight is within 5 km of an aerodrome
options.why: AP2 is only for recreation or education. The 5 km condition is what makes HOBBYISTS need AP2.

options.text: A UA Operator Permit and a Class 2 Activity Permit
options.why: An OP is always paired with AP1. There is no OP + AP2 combination.

options.text: A UA Operator Permit and a Class 1 Activity Permit, with the location assessed as part of the AP1
options.why: Business flying always needs OP + AP1. The 5 km location goes into the AP1 application and gets a stricter assessment; no AP2 is added.

options.text: A UA Operator Permit, a Class 1 and a Class 2 Activity Permit
options.why: You never hold both for one activity. AP1 covers the business flight, including its location.

note: WHY you fly decides AP1 vs AP2. WHERE you fly only decides whether a hobbyist needs AP2.

question: A student flies a 5 kg UA for an education purpose at 250 ft AMSL. What permit is needed?

options.text: A UA Operator Permit and a Class 1 Activity Permit
options.why: For education, OP + AP1 starts above 7 kg (or for BVLOS). At 5 kg the height condition triggers AP2 instead.

options.text: No permit, because educational flights are exempt from height limits
options.why: Education up to 7 kg follows the same AP2 conditions as recreation, including the 200 ft AMSL limit.

options.text: A Class 2 Activity Permit
options.why: Education with a UA of 7 kg or less needs AP2 when flown above 200 ft AMSL (reg 8(2)).

options.text: A Class B UAPL
options.why: Class B is a pilot licence for UA over 25 kg, not a permit for an activity.

question: Which situation needs a UA Operator Permit and a Class 1 Activity Permit for a hobbyist flying a 1 kg drone?

options.text: Flying above 200 ft AMSL
options.why: Height above 200 ft AMSL is an AP2 condition for recreation.

options.text: Flying beyond visual line of sight
options.why: BVLOS needs OP + AP1 regardless of purpose or mass.

options.text: Flying within 5 km of an aerodrome
options.why: For recreation, proximity to an aerodrome triggers AP2, not OP + AP1.

options.text: Flying in a danger area
options.why: A restricted or danger area is an AP2 condition for recreation up to 25 kg.

source: AC 101-2-1 (Rev 8) paras 2.2(d), 2.3; CAAS 'Requirements for flying UA' page
